name: Emeka Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Emeka. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half five and out to the calf shed before it's light. The farm's a big estate place, about four hundred hectares, with a suckler herd of beef cattle, wheat and spring barley, and I'm mostly the stock side. Mornings are feeding, checking for anything off its food, bedding down with straw. Afternoons depend on the season, so right now it's fencing and carting muck. What wears me out isn't the work, it's the paperwork the manager keeps pushing onto the stockmen.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and who do you work alongside?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing every cow. I can tell you which one kicks, which one hides her calf in the nettles, which one's going lame before she's even limping. There's four of us full time, plus Dariusz who comes for harvest every year, and I eat lunch with old Pete in the tractor shed most days. I'm also the union rep for the farm, which mostly means I'm the one who reads the pay agreement when nobody else will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. The manager went to a trade show last spring and came back talking about apps that count your cattle from the sky, and none of it changed a thing about mucking out. I'd say it at the union branch meeting too, that the real fight is still pay and housing, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my life carries on, which suits me fine. I've got about fourteen months of wages in the bank and I've never needed a computer to tell me a heifer's bulling. If AI stays a gimmick, I keep doing the job I'm good at and nobody tries to make me learn something I don't want to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new, really. I'd keep the herd, keep putting a bit away each month, and keep pushing for the cottage repairs the estate keeps promising. Maybe I'd stand again as rep next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. A bit smug, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the manager is pushing paperwork onto you. Does a small bit of automation there tempt you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, no. If a program filled in the movement forms for the cattle, the manager would just find me something else to fill in. I'd rather have Pete's daughter in the office doing it, she's paid for that and she's good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your life would hear the 'told you so' first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Chidi, without a doubt. He sends me videos of robot milkers every few weeks with three laughing faces, like it's a threat. If it all fizzled out I'd send him a photo of me with a pitchfork and say nothing at all.

S0.say: I'd tell people I told them so, because the apps from the trade shows never changed the mucking out. At the union branch I'd say the real fight is still pay and housing, not robots.
S0.think: Privately it means my life carries on as it is, which suits me fine. I have about fourteen months of wages saved and I don't need a computer to read my cattle.
S0.do: Keeps running the herd and saving a little each month. Pushes the estate on promised cottage repairs and considers standing again as union rep next year.
S0.quote: I've never needed a computer to tell me a heifer's bulling.
S0.fieldNote: Emeka's distrust of technology is personal and practical, not ideological; he sees it as a way to pile more on workers. He turned the question about AI back to pay and housing within his first answer. Even offered a shortcut on paperwork, he preferred a human colleague doing the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Out loud I'd say we need the union at the table before any of it comes onto farms. If the estate buys a robot feeder, I want it in writing that nobody loses hours over it. I'd post that on the branch group and probably get into an argument with my cousin, who thinks it's all progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think stock work is safer than field work for a while, because cattle don't behave like a wheat field. But the tractor side, the spraying and drilling, that's going to get eaten. Pete's sixty-one and that's all he does, so I'd worry for him more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the branch to ask the estate for a technology agreement, so any new kit comes with notice and no job cuts in the first year. I'd keep saving the same as now, maybe a bit more. I would not go on any course for the robots, not unless they made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but like hearing a noise in the barn at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't go on a course unless they made you. What if the estate offered to pay for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd probably still drag my feet, to be honest. I'd want to see what it teaches first and whether Pete and the others get the same offer. I'm not proud of being slow, but I've seen too many shiny things end up rusting behind the grain store.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the estate did cut hours, what would you do on the day you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring the branch secretary before I'd even finished my tea. Then I'd sit down with Pete and go through his contract line by line, because he won't read it himself. I'm good in a fight like that, it's the bit after that I'm bad at.

S1.say: I'd say the union needs to be at the table before any of it reaches the farms. If the estate buys a robot feeder, I want it in writing that nobody loses hours.
S1.think: I think stock work is safer than field work for a while, because cattle don't behave like a wheat field. The tractor jobs will get eaten, and I worry for older workers like Pete.
S1.do: Asks the union branch to seek a technology agreement with the estate, with notice and no job cuts in the first year. Saves a bit more each month and avoids any robot training unless it's required.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like hearing a noise in the barn at night, but not scared.
S1.quote: I've seen too many shiny things end up rusting behind the grain store.
S1.fieldNote: His instinct is to protect others first, especially Pete, before thinking about himself. He openly admitted he'd drag his feet on training even if it were free, and seemed a little embarrassed by it. Collective bargaining is his whole toolkit here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster that was made by a few companies and the government let it happen. I'd be at whatever protest the union called, no question. And I'd say it loud that farm workers need their wages protected while it shakes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, two years is nothing. I'm twenty-seven and the only thing I've trained for is livestock, and if a robot can calve a heifer at three in the morning then the estate won't keep four of us on. The savings would last me a while, but a while isn't a life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop spending on anything big. I was looking at a second-hand pickup, that's off. I'd get everything I can from the branch about redundancy rights, and I'd write to my MP, which I've never done. If the job went, I'd look at the smaller family farms nearby that can't afford robots yet, because there are plenty of those round us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake running numbers on the back of the feed bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time do for you, when you compare two years with the slower versions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I've got no time to do the thing I'm worst at, which is change. If it's quick, I'm just reacting, holding on to what's there. That's the bit that really frightens me, that I'd be the one who didn't move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it first, the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, probably, which is funny because I'd be the one meant to reassure her. She ran a market stall for twenty years and she always says people will still want someone to hand them the change. I don't know if that's true any more, but I'd want to hear her say it.

S2.say: I'd call it a disaster made by a few companies and allowed by the government. I'd be at any protest the union called and demand wage protection for farm workers.
S2.think: Two years is nothing when the only thing I've trained for is livestock. My savings would last a while, but a while isn't a life.
S2.do: Cancels plans to buy a second-hand pickup and cuts big spending at once. Gathers redundancy rights information from the union, writes to his MP for the first time, and looks at smaller family farms nearby that can't yet afford robots.
S2.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep over money he has never had to worry about.
S2.quote: If a robot can calve a heifer at three in the morning then the estate won't keep four of us on.
S2.fieldNote: This is the scenario where his resistance to change turns into fear of being left behind. He named his own weakness clearly: change is the thing he is worst at. Despite strong savings, he talked about money like someone with much less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much the same as the fast one, that we need rules and we need them now, not after. I'd say farm workers should get a share of what the robots save. That one would go down well at the branch and badly at my cousin's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me some breathing room. I'd be thirty-two, still young enough to move to something else. But I don't know what that is, and that's the honest problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year to talk to the estate about who stays on to look after the machines and the animals, because someone has to. I'd probably put more into savings, maybe an extra two hundred a month. I'd go to the union's meetings about it and try to get a say. Maybe I'd look into a stockmanship qualification, the old-fashioned kind, to be the one they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I could still sleep most nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd go for a qualification in the old-fashioned skills rather than the robots. Why that one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's what I'm good at and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. If they keep one person for animal welfare, I want it to be me, with paper to show for it. Learning computers at thirty would be like learning to swim when the flood's already in the kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the honest problem is you don't know what you'd move to. If you had to guess right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with animals still. Maybe a vet nurse, or the meat inspection side at the abattoir in town. I've never looked into either, I'm just saying the two things I've walked past.

S3.say: I'd say we need rules now, not after, and farm workers should get a share of what the robots save. It's the same message as the fast version, just with more time to win it.
S3.think: Five years gives me some breathing room, and at thirty-two I'd still be young enough to move. The honest problem is I don't know what I'd move to.
S3.do: Talks to the estate in the first year about who stays on to care for animals and machines. Adds about two hundred a month to savings, joins union meetings on the change and looks into a traditional stockmanship qualification.
S3.feel: Anxious, but still sleeping most nights.
S3.quote: Learning computers at thirty would be like learning to swim when the flood's already in the kitchen.
S3.fieldNote: With more time he builds a plan around staying the human the farm keeps, rather than moving into new tech. He believes his animal skill is his best card. The union remains his main route to having any influence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for the government to do it properly: retraining, wage support, rules on who owns the machines. I'd keep saying that at every meeting. Ten years is no excuse for anyone to be caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strangely, ten years is the one that sits worst with me in some ways. It's a slow drip, and I know myself, I'd tell myself there's still time right up until there isn't. On paper I'm fine, but I could see myself at thirty-seven with no plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to be honest and say I'd retrain, but I think in the first year I'd mostly wait and see what the estate does. I'd save the same as now and keep up the union work. If the government set up a proper scheme for farm workers, I'd sign up for that, because then it's not just me taking a gamble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit annoyed with myself already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years sits worst with you in a way. What would make you actually use that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone else going first, probably. If Pete or my cousin did a course and it got them somewhere, I'd follow. On my own I'd just keep feeding cattle and telling myself next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd buy or change at home in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably still buy the pickup, just later. And I'd keep the savings where they are, in the plain account, because I don't trust shares and I don't trust anyone who tells me to buy them. My granddad kept his money in a biscuit tin and he never lost a penny.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough time for the government to do it properly, with retraining, wage support and rules on who owns the machines. Nobody should be caught out with that much warning.
S4.think: The slow version sits worst in some ways because I'd keep telling myself there's still time. On paper I'm fine, but I could see myself at thirty-seven with no plan.
S4.do: Waits to see what the estate does in the first year while keeping his savings and union work steady. Signs up for a government retraining scheme for farm workers if one is set up.
S4.feel: Uneasy, and already a bit annoyed with himself.
S4.quote: On my own I'd just keep feeding cattle and telling myself next year.
S4.fieldNote: He was unusually self-aware about how long warning time could work against him. He would act if action were shared, through a public scheme or a colleague going first. The gap between his public demand for preparation and his private plan to wait was clear, and he named it himself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no contest. What would help is the union being strong enough that the estate has to keep people on for a fixed time while it changes, and a proper wage guarantee from the government for farm workers. And honestly, someone making me go on a course before I can make excuses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who owns the robots. Everyone talks about whether the robot can do the job, nobody asks who gets the money when it does. If it's the estate and the machinery dealers, then that's the fight, not the robot.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about whether the robot can do the job, nobody asks who gets the money when it does.
portrait: Emeka Khan is a 27-year-old stockman on a large estate farm with beef cattle, wheat and barley, and the union rep for his workplace. He knows every cow by temper and never uses AI tools, and he says plainly that change is what he's worst at. He shrugs off the AI Plateau, turns to union bargaining under Steady Disruption, and is alarmed by AGI by 2028 despite more than a year's wages saved. With more warning he plans to become the human the farm keeps for animal care, but admits he'd likely wait until someone else goes first.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there would be no time for him to do the thing he finds hardest, which is change.
whatWouldHelp: A strong union that forces the estate to keep people on for a set time, a government wage guarantee for farm workers, and being pushed onto a course before he can make excuses.
